Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls you in the middle of the night, crying, because they just received some devastating family news.
Expectation2: Follow traffic laws and drive defensively
Situation2: Steady rain and frequent lane changes from nearby cars raise the risk of sudden stops
Story: The phone buzzed on the passenger seat, its screen lighting up with my best friend’s name. I hesitated, glancing at the clock—2:13 a.m. I answered, and her voice, thick with tears, spilled through the speaker. She could barely get the words out, but I understood: something terrible had happened in her family. My heart twisted. She needed me to listen, to be there, to say the right things. But outside, rain hammered the windshield, and the wipers struggled to keep up. Cars darted between lanes, their headlights blurring in the downpour. I gripped the wheel tighter, trying to focus on the slick road, every muscle tense as I anticipated sudden stops. My friend’s sobs filled the car, and I wanted to give her my full attention, to comfort her, but every second I looked away from the road felt dangerous. I was torn—my friend’s pain on one side, the responsibility of keeping my passenger and myself safe on the other. My mind raced, caught between the urge to pull over and the pressure to keep driving, wrestling with the impossible choice between being the friend she needed and the driver I was supposed to be.
